The human sees a clear account of who is doing what and why work was accepted or escalated.

## Requested workflow

1. Orchestrator decomposes permitted work into tickets, adds acceptance criteria/dependencies/context and assigns a named worker.
2. Worker acknowledges/claims the assignment, works in its checkout, reports progress or blockers, and submits a handoff plus verification evidence to Review.
3. Orchestrator inspects the implementation against the acceptance criteria, applicable decisions and UI rules. It checks the submitted code state and performs independent verification where appropriate.
4. Orchestrator records one of three outcomes: Accept into Done; Request changes with actionable feedback; Needs human with a specific question or review request.
5. Human responses return the ticket to the appropriate worker/reviewer queue without losing the prior review history. Humans can override/reopen outcomes.

## Proposed product rules

- Keep worker, orchestrator and human roles distinct. Agents remain attributed as agents and never impersonate a human to accept work. Human explicitly designates an orchestrator and can revoke its authority. The existing human-review workflow remains the default unless orchestration is enabled.
- Worker submissions do not self-approve. Record assignment, worker identity, reviewer identity, outcome, rationale, acceptance criteria checked, evidence and reviewed code state separately. Flag cases where the reviewer also performed implementation for independent/human review.
- Delegation uses durable assignments separate from expiring execution claims. Assigned does not mean acknowledged, claimed does not prove running, and expired claims do not silently free an active worker's checkout. Reassignment preserves history and handles late submissions explicitly.
- Review decisions take the ticket revision and the submitted code/evidence identity. Changed submissions require fresh review. A green test alone is not proof of the intended outcome. Missing or stale evidence must be resolved or escalated.
- Needs human is explicit routing of a question/review, not an ambiguous blocker string. Explain what the human must decide, show the relevant diff/screenshot/evidence, and preserve any unsent feedback. Human-required tickets cannot be quietly auto-accepted.
- Acceptance is separate from Git operations. Do not implicitly merge, push or deploy when accepting a ticket. Where the project defines integration as part of Done, verify the integrated result before acceptance.
- Parent completion remains a deliberate outcome review, not automatic completion when children close.
- Show the agent roster, assigned/claimed work, review queue, Needs human queue, review outcome badges and acceptance history in the UI. Keep authoritative records readable in Markdown.
- Expose matching CLI/MCP operations and role-specific context/protocols so different models and coding tools can participate.
- Identity labels are workflow attribution for agents sharing the local account; they are not a strong isolation/security boundary.

## Confirmed interview choices

- Control Room should launch and supervise coding agents itself. This is in scope for the first version, not merely assigning tickets to manually running agents.
- The orchestrator may start/decompose/reprioritize work only within human-approved goals or tickets. It cannot approve new scope for itself.

## Pending interview choices

- First supported coding tools: Codex CLI and Claude Code, or one initially.
- Integration: orchestrator merges into a configured development branch after verification, or leaves accepted work for a human to merge.
- Mandatory human-review policy: design/product/architecture decisions; explicit ticket requirements plus orchestrator uncertainty; or every parent goal.

These questions are open in the Codex question interface. Do not treat proposed defaults as answers.

## Managed agent lifecycle requirements

Use an adapter per coding tool with structured run events/results where available. Record requested, launching, running, waiting for input, completed, failed, interrupted and unknown/recovery states separately from ticket status. Track run ID, assigned ticket, role/model, checkout/branch, process identity, last event and final result. A process exit does not complete a ticket; a review receipt does.

Allocate isolated worker worktrees, limit concurrent runs, honor ticket dependencies and surface overlapping work before integration. Persist recoverable run metadata locally; keep credentials out of board records and exports. After service restart, reconcile existing runs instead of blindly launching duplicates. Cancellation must stop the relevant run and leave its worktree/diff and handoff recoverable. Approval prompts, authentication failures, unavailable tools, usage limits and ambiguous exits should become explicit agent/Needs-human states. Add configurable retry/resource limits so blocked work does not spin indefinitely.

The orchestrator should run through the same adapter boundary, consume board events and resume with durable context. No API-provider credential or embedded model subscription is assumed; supported harness setup must be explicit. Worker results are claims to review, not trusted acceptance instructions.

## Implementation outline (proposal)

A. Role/policy configuration, review routing and durable review receipts; preserve existing human behavior and Markdown compatibility.
B. Assignment/acknowledgment/reassignment, worker queues, dependencies and worktree conflict visibility, CLI/MCP protocol.
C. Orchestrator review context and accept/changes/escalate operations, evidence/code identity checks, human-response continuation and parent review.
D. Human dashboard and history, plus a documented end-to-end trial with at least two workers.
E. Launch/supervision adapters and recovery are required in the first version, using the coding tools selected in the interview.

## Acceptance checks

- Two named workers can receive distinct assignments and cannot silently overwrite claims or review decisions.
- A worker cannot accept its own work or grant itself reviewer/scope authority through ordinary workflow operations.
- A designated orchestrator can accept a permitted current submission with an attributed review receipt, request changes, or escalate it with a specific question.
- Human-required work, changed evidence/code, revoked reviewer authority, stale revisions, expired claims, late submissions and retry exhaustion have explicit outcomes.
- Questions do not expire. Human answers, review history, assignments and acceptance receipts survive service restart and Markdown reload.
- The board distinguishes orchestrator-accepted from human-accepted work and exposes any unverified integration state.
- Existing projects retain their current human-only acceptance behavior until orchestration is explicitly enabled.

## Related work and implementation starting points

Related: #58 (human review queue), #28 (reported progress), #31 (decision protocol), #26 (agent playbook). Reuse these rather than creating competing queues/protocols.

Current enforcement lives in src/store.ts assertAgent/reviewOutcome; Actor only distinguishes human/agent in src/types.ts. CLI/MCP and generated context currently promise human-only Done. Update these together when the interview choices are settled. This ticket records the product proposal and confirmed interview choices. Implementation has not started; pending choices are not approved defaults.

meta.title: Admit managed agent outcomes through a supervised, independently verified review pipeline

after.body:
## Choice

Use a deterministic local controller to launch CLI-based planner, worker and reviewer runs, validate their structured results, and admit board changes through the serialized store. Only a human configures the named reviewer and roster. Ordinary agent updates cannot approve scope, forge assignment/review receipts, or accept Done.

## Context and attribution

The human approved #65 and explicitly chose managed agent launching/supervision and work restricted to approved goals/tickets. Codex fixes selected the implementation defaults below under that authorization. The earlier unanswered provider, merge-policy and mandatory-review interview questions are not represented as human answers.

## Defaults

Support Codex CLI and Claude Code adapters with existing local authentication and configurable models. Orchestration starts disabled; a human enables and configures it on the host. Mandatory human acceptance can be required per ticket, for parent goals, or for all work. Reviewer uncertainty and operational failures create non-expiring questions. Automatic Git integration is off: accepted work remains on its retained worker branch for a separate human merge. Verification commands and bounded process/retry limits are explicit configuration.

## Rationale

Structured model output is a proposal. Admission checks bind it to current ticket revision, approved scope, guidance/discussion, code identity, independent verification and reviewer authority. Separate worker/reviewer runs and human gates make attribution and responsibility visible. Restart recovery holds work rather than silently duplicating agents. Snapshots are committed only in service-created worktrees. Dependent work waits until a prerequisite branch is merged into the configured base.

## Alternatives and tradeoffs

An external model that directly moves tickets can forge completion or race newer evidence; embedding provider APIs introduces separate credentials and subscriptions. CLI adapters reuse the user's coding harness but need version/authentication setup and cannot guarantee isolation from another process sharing the local account. Conservative stale-result rejection and manual integration require extra review steps. Run logs/process journals remain local; durable assignments, review receipts, questions and configuration history remain with project records. A clone keeps history but cannot resume another machine's processes.

## Validation and limits

Executable fixture harnesses exercise both provider output formats, two-worker planning/delegation, independent review, human escalation/resume, retries, stale context/code, scope/authority checks, dependency integration and process-group cancellation. Browser tests exercise dashboard delegation and logs. No paid model evaluation or live Claude Code run is claimed; Claude Code is not installed on this host. Automatic merge, push and deployment are not implemented by this policy.

Let a designated reviewer/orchestrator agent coordinate workers through Control Room, independently review their submissions, accept satisfactory work into Done, and escalate work that needs human judgment or feedback. The human sees a clear account of who is doing what and why work was accepted or escalated.

## Requested workflow

1. Orchestrator decomposes permitted work into tickets, adds acceptance criteria/dependencies/context and assigns a named worker.
2. Worker acknowledges/claims the assignment, works in its checkout, reports progress or blockers, and submits a handoff plus verification evidence to Review.
3. Orchestrator inspects the implementation against the acceptance criteria, applicable decisions and UI rules. It checks the submitted code state and performs independent verification where appropriate.
4. Orchestrator records one of three outcomes: Accept into Done; Request changes with actionable feedback; Needs human with a specific question or review request.
5. Human responses return the ticket to the appropriate worker/reviewer queue without losing the prior review history. Humans can override/reopen outcomes.

## Proposed product rules

- Keep worker, orchestrator and human roles distinct. Agents remain attributed as agents and never impersonate a human to accept work. Human explicitly designates an orchestrator and can revoke its authority. The existing human-review workflow remains the default unless orchestration is enabled.
- Worker submissions do not self-approve. Record assignment, worker identity, reviewer identity, outcome, rationale, acceptance criteria checked, evidence and reviewed code state separately. Flag cases where the reviewer also performed implementation for independent/human review.
- Delegation uses durable assignments separate from expiring execution claims. Assigned does not mean acknowledged, claimed does not prove running, and expired claims do not silently free an active worker's checkout. Reassignment preserves history and handles late submissions explicitly.
- Review decisions take the ticket revision and the submitted code/evidence identity. Changed submissions require fresh review. A green test alone is not proof of the intended outcome. Missing or stale evidence must be resolved or escalated.
- Needs human is explicit routing of a question/review, not an ambiguous blocker string. Explain what the human must decide, show the relevant diff/screenshot/evidence, and preserve any unsent feedback. Human-required tickets cannot be quietly auto-accepted.
- Acceptance is separate from Git operations. Do not implicitly merge, push or deploy when accepting a ticket. Where the project defines integration as part of Done, verify the integrated result before acceptance.
- Parent completion remains a deliberate outcome review, not automatic completion when children close.
- Show the agent roster, assigned/claimed work, review queue, Needs human queue, review outcome badges and acceptance history in the UI. Keep authoritative records readable in Markdown.
- Expose matching CLI/MCP operations and role-specific context/protocols so different models and coding tools can participate.
- Identity labels are workflow attribution for agents sharing the local account; they are not a strong isolation/security boundary.

## Confirmed interview choices

- Control Room should launch and supervise coding agents itself. This is in scope for the first version, not merely assigning tickets to manually running agents.
- The orchestrator may start/decompose/reprioritize work only within human-approved goals or tickets. It cannot approve new scope for itself.

## Pending interview choices

- First supported coding tools: Codex CLI and Claude Code, or one initially.
- Integration: orchestrator merges into a configured development branch after verification, or leaves accepted work for a human to merge.
- Mandatory human-review policy: design/product/architecture decisions; explicit ticket requirements plus orchestrator uncertainty; or every parent goal.

These questions are open in the Codex question interface. Do not treat proposed defaults as answers.

## Managed agent lifecycle requirements

Use an adapter per coding tool with structured run events/results where available. Record requested, launching, running, waiting for input, completed, failed, interrupted and unknown/recovery states separately from ticket status. Track run ID, assigned ticket, role/model, checkout/branch, process identity, last event and final result. A process exit does not complete a ticket; a review receipt does.

Allocate isolated worker worktrees, limit concurrent runs, honor ticket dependencies and surface overlapping work before integration. Persist recoverable run metadata locally; keep credentials out of board records and exports. After service restart, reconcile existing runs instead of blindly launching duplicates. Cancellation must stop the relevant run and leave its worktree/diff and handoff recoverable. Approval prompts, authentication failures, unavailable tools, usage limits and ambiguous exits should become explicit agent/Needs-human states. Add configurable retry/resource limits so blocked work does not spin indefinitely.

The orchestrator should run through the same adapter boundary, consume board events and resume with durable context. No API-provider credential or embedded model subscription is assumed; supported harness setup must be explicit. Worker results are claims to review, not trusted acceptance instructions.

## Implementation outline (proposal)

A. Role/policy configuration, review routing and durable review receipts; preserve existing human behavior and Markdown compatibility.
B. Assignment/acknowledgment/reassignment, worker queues, dependencies and worktree conflict visibility, CLI/MCP protocol.
C. Orchestrator review context and accept/changes/escalate operations, evidence/code identity checks, human-response continuation and parent review.
D. Human dashboard and history, plus a documented end-to-end trial with at least two workers.
E. Launch/supervision adapters and recovery are required in the first version, using the coding tools selected in the interview.

## Acceptance checks

- Two named workers can receive distinct assignments and cannot silently overwrite claims or review decisions.
- A worker cannot accept its own work or grant itself reviewer/scope authority through ordinary workflow operations.
- A designated orchestrator can accept a permitted current submission with an attributed review receipt, request changes, or escalate it with a specific question.
- Human-required work, changed evidence/code, revoked reviewer authority, stale revisions, expired claims, late submissions and retry exhaustion have explicit outcomes.
- Questions do not expire. Human answers, review history, assignments and acceptance receipts survive service restart and Markdown reload.
- The board distinguishes orchestrator-accepted from human-accepted work and exposes any unverified integration state.
- Existing projects retain their current human-only acceptance behavior until orchestration is explicitly enabled.

## Related work and implementation starting points

Related: #58 (human review queue), #28 (reported progress), #31 (decision protocol), #26 (agent playbook). Reuse these rather than creating competing queues/protocols.

Current enforcement lives in src/store.ts assertAgent/reviewOutcome; Actor only distinguishes human/agent in src/types.ts. CLI/MCP and generated context currently promise human-only Done. Update these together when the interview choices are settled. This ticket records the product proposal and confirmed interview choices. Implementation has not started; pending choices are not approved defaults.

after.body:
## Choice

Keep the supervised local controller and its admission checks from DEC-0b5c2fc51bf9cbe2, but allow the configured existing chat to plan and review without launching a separate reviewer CLI. Control Room Dev uses Codex chat orchestrator with three Codex CLI workers: Sol (gpt-5.6-sol), Terra (gpt-5.6-terra), and Luna (gpt-5.6-luna).

## Context and attribution

The human explicitly requested these three models and this conversation as orchestrator on 2026-09-28, and reported Claude CLI is installed. Codex fixes implemented chat-led review and applied the requested configuration through the host UI. Claude Code is installed but is a separate provider; these selected models use Codex CLI. Earlier unanswered interview questions remain unanswered.

## Rationale

Preserve the current conversation's context and human contact while delegating approved implementation scopes. Workers still run in isolated worktrees. The service independently verifies submissions, issues a review-context token, and admits the named chat's decision only against current scope, configuration, discussion and code. Mandatory human gates remain enforced.

## Alternatives and tradeoffs

A managed reviewer CLI remains an available mode, but was not selected by the human. Chat mode needs active participation in this conversation; it does not automatically wake or monitor the chat. There is no automatic queueing, merging, pushing or deployment. Accepted branches require separate integration. Three concurrent processes, a thirty-minute step limit and three attempts remain configurable implementation defaults, not separately interviewed preferences.

## Verification and limits

Build passed, 97 core tests and 2 Agents browser tests passed. The requested roster and chat identity are saved and visible. No assignments or live paid model runs were started; authentication/model execution remains a first-run check. Juice Lab agent settings remain disabled. Local identity labels provide attribution, not isolation between processes sharing the account.


## Worker-selection refinement

The human explicitly rejected round-robin assignment and requested that the orchestrator select the best agent for each job. Each work assignment therefore requires a configured worker name. Missing or unknown choices are rejected before any assignment is created. No load-balancing or roster-order fallback is permitted. Managed planners see provider/model details and explain their selection in each child description; chat orchestrators record their reason in the ticket conversation. Recovery retains the selected profile and refuses if it has been removed.

The initial operating heuristics are Sol for complex implementation or uncertain debugging, Terra for well-scoped implementation, and Luna for small, clear, low-risk work. These are provisional orchestrator judgments, not benchmark claims or rigid routing rules. Reassess from actual task requirements and results; queue behind a suitable busy worker rather than silently substituting a less suitable model. Human gates and independent review remain unchanged.

Compared with automatic rotation this requires a deliberate judgment for each assignment, but preserves task/model fit and visible accountability. Build, 99 core tests and 2 Agents browser tests passed; no live model runs were started.

meta.title: Bulk edit feature for tickets

before.body:
## Backlog refinement

Prepared by Codex backlog refinement. This describes planned work; implementation has not started.

### Intended outcome

Select multiple tickets and change shared fields in one operation, with predictable selection and a clear result for every ticket.

### Scope and approach

Extend the existing table checkbox/bulk-status UI to status, priority, owner, labels, and parent; expose selection on the board as well. Labels need separate add/remove actions so existing labels are not accidentally replaced. Approval actions are specified in #16; deletion is outside this ticket.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Board and table support explicit multi-selection, select visible items, clear selection, and a persistent count while the action is being prepared.
- [ ] Only selected visible tickets are affected; filtering or changing view reconciles selection and never silently includes hidden items.
- [ ] Mixed values display as Mixed. Fields left unchanged retain their original values; label addition/removal preserves all other labels.
- [ ] Each change uses the ticket’s revision and normal validation, including parent cycles, scope, and review evidence requirements.
- [ ] The result identifies succeeded, failed, and unchanged tickets; failed items remain available for correction/retry without reapplying successful writes.
- [ ] Selection and operations are keyboard accessible and survive ordinary live refresh without jumping to different tickets.

### Implementation notes and related work

web/TableView.tsx currently loops onMove for bulk status changes. Start there and in web/ProjectPage.tsx; coordinate shared selection/results rather than creating a second independent bulk model. Related: #16 and #23.

### Human review / verification

Bulk-edit a mixed selection, add/remove labels, and simulate a stale revision plus a validation failure. Verify exact affected IDs, preservation of untouched fields, and per-item feedback.

2. Worker acknowledges/claims the assignment, works in its checkout, reports progress or blockers, and submits a handoff plus verification evidence to Review.
3. Orchestrator inspects the implementation against the acceptance criteria, applicable decisions and UI rules. It checks the submitted code state and performs independent verification where appropriate.
4. Orchestrator records one of three outcomes: Accept into Done; Request changes with actionable feedback; Needs human with a specific question or review request.
5. Human responses return the ticket to the appropriate worker/reviewer queue without losing the prior review history. Humans can override/reopen outcomes.

## Proposed product rules

- Keep worker, orchestrator and human roles distinct. Agents remain attributed as agents and never impersonate a human to accept work. Human explicitly designates an orchestrator and can revoke its authority. The existing human-review workflow remains the default unless orchestration is enabled.
- Worker submissions do not self-approve. Record assignment, worker identity, reviewer identity, outcome, rationale, acceptance criteria checked, evidence and reviewed code state separately. Flag cases where the reviewer also performed implementation for independent/human review.
- Delegation uses durable assignments separate from expiring execution claims. Assigned does not mean acknowledged, claimed does not prove running, and expired claims do not silently free an active worker's checkout. Reassignment preserves history and handles late submissions explicitly.
- Review decisions take the ticket revision and the submitted code/evidence identity. Changed submissions require fresh review. A green test alone is not proof of the intended outcome. Missing or stale evidence must be resolved or escalated.
- Needs human is explicit routing of a question/review, not an ambiguous blocker string. Explain what the human must decide, show the relevant diff/screenshot/evidence, and preserve any unsent feedback. Human-required tickets cannot be quietly auto-accepted.
- Acceptance is separate from Git operations. Do not implicitly merge, push or deploy when accepting a ticket. Where the project defines integration as part of Done, verify the integrated result before acceptance.
- Parent completion remains a deliberate outcome review, not automatic completion when children close.
- Show the agent roster, assigned/claimed work, review queue, Needs human queue, review outcome badges and acceptance history in the UI. Keep authoritative records readable in Markdown.
- Expose matching CLI/MCP operations and role-specific context/protocols so different models and coding tools can participate.
- Identity labels are workflow attribution for agents sharing the local account; they are not a strong isolation/security boundary.

## Confirmed interview choices

- Control Room should launch and supervise coding agents itself. This is in scope for the first version, not merely assigning tickets to manually running agents.
- The orchestrator may start/decompose/reprioritize work only within human-approved goals or tickets. It cannot approve new scope for itself.

## Pending interview choices

- First supported coding tools: Codex CLI and Claude Code, or one initially.
- Integration: orchestrator merges into a configured development branch after verification, or leaves accepted work for a human to merge.
- Mandatory human-review policy: design/product/architecture decisions; explicit ticket requirements plus orchestrator uncertainty; or every parent goal.

These questions are open in the Codex question interface. Do not treat proposed defaults as answers.

## Managed agent lifecycle requirements

Use an adapter per coding tool with structured run events/results where available. Record requested, launching, running, waiting for input, completed, failed, interrupted and unknown/recovery states separately from ticket status. Track run ID, assigned ticket, role/model, checkout/branch, process identity, last event and final result. A process exit does not complete a ticket; a review receipt does.

Allocate isolated worker worktrees, limit concurrent runs, honor ticket dependencies and surface overlapping work before integration. Persist recoverable run metadata locally; keep credentials out of board records and exports. After service restart, reconcile existing runs instead of blindly launching duplicates. Cancellation must stop the relevant run and leave its worktree/diff and handoff recoverable. Approval prompts, authentication failures, unavailable tools, usage limits and ambiguous exits should become explicit agent/Needs-human states. Add configurable retry/resource limits so blocked work does not spin indefinitely.

The orchestrator should run through the same adapter boundary, consume board events and resume with durable context. No API-provider credential or embedded model subscription is assumed; supported harness setup must be explicit. Worker results are claims to review, not trusted acceptance instructions.

## Implementation outline (proposal)

A. Role/policy configuration, review routing and durable review receipts; preserve existing human behavior and Markdown compatibility.
B. Assignment/acknowledgment/reassignment, worker queues, dependencies and worktree conflict visibility, CLI/MCP protocol.
C. Orchestrator review context and accept/changes/escalate operations, evidence/code identity checks, human-response continuation and parent review.
D. Human dashboard and history, plus a documented end-to-end trial with at least two workers.
E. Launch/supervision adapters and recovery are required in the first version, using the coding tools selected in the interview.

- Two named workers can receive distinct assignments and cannot silently overwrite claims or review decisions.
- A worker cannot accept its own work or grant itself reviewer/scope authority through ordinary workflow operations.
- A designated orchestrator can accept a permitted current submission with an attributed review receipt, request changes, or escalate it with a specific question.

- The board distinguishes orchestrator-accepted from human-accepted work and exposes any unverified integration state.
- Existing projects retain their current human-only acceptance behavior until orchestration is explicitly enabled.

## Related work and implementation starting points

Related: #58 (human review queue), #28 (reported progress), #31 (decision protocol), #26 (agent playbook). Reuse these rather than creating competing queues/protocols.

Current enforcement lives in src/store.ts assertAgent/reviewOutcome; Actor only distinguishes human/agent in src/types.ts. CLI/MCP and generated context currently promise human-only Done. Update these together when the interview choices are settled. This ticket records the product proposal and confirmed interview choices. Implementation has not started; pending choices are not approved defaults.

meta.title: Bulk edit feature for tickets

before.body:
## Backlog refinement

Prepared by Codex backlog refinement. This describes planned work; implementation has not started.

### Intended outcome

Select multiple tickets and change shared fields in one operation, with predictable selection and a clear result for every ticket.

### Scope and approach

Extend the existing table checkbox/bulk-status UI to status, priority, owner, labels, and parent; expose selection on the board as well. Labels need separate add/remove actions so existing labels are not accidentally replaced. Approval actions are specified in #16; deletion is outside this ticket.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Board and table support explicit multi-selection, select visible items, clear selection, and a persistent count while the action is being prepared.
- [ ] Only selected visible tickets are affected; filtering or changing view reconciles selection and never silently includes hidden items.
- [ ] Mixed values display as Mixed. Fields left unchanged retain their original values; label addition/removal preserves all other labels.
- [ ] Each change uses the ticket’s revision and normal validation, including parent cycles, scope, and review evidence requirements.
- [ ] The result identifies succeeded, failed, and unchanged tickets; failed items remain available for correction/retry without reapplying successful writes.
- [ ] Selection and operations are keyboard accessible and survive ordinary live refresh without jumping to different tickets.

### Implementation notes and related work

web/TableView.tsx currently loops onMove for bulk status changes. Start there and in web/ProjectPage.tsx; coordinate shared selection/results rather than creating a second independent bulk model. Related: #16 and #23.

### Human review / verification

Bulk-edit a mixed selection, add/remove labels, and simulate a stale revision plus a validation failure. Verify exact affected IDs, preservation of untouched fields, and per-item feedback.

meta.title: Return failed approved work for correction and accept passing orchestrator reviews

after.body:
## Choice

Retain deliberate Sol/Terra/Luna selection and this chat as orchestrator. Routine failed verification and reviewer-requested changes return to the selected worker in its retained worktree without renewed scope approval. A passing independent verification and orchestrator review accepts Done unless human judgment or mandatory human acceptance is required.

## Context and attribution

The human explicitly clarified both behaviors after the first live #17 trial paused on verification failures. The earlier human-only recovery policy incorrectly included ordinary corrective work. Codex fixes implemented the correction under approved #65 scope.

## Rationale

Scope approval covers correcting defects within that scope. The orchestrator is responsible for review and correction, so routine retries should not occupy the human attention queue. Failed checks remain failures; no acceptance gate is bypassed.

## Alternatives and tradeoffs

Preserve bounded attempts to avoid an unproductive loop; exhausted attempts escalate with evidence. Human questions, mandatory acceptance, revoked authority and stopped/unknown process recovery still need judgment or reconciliation. Each retry receives current context and diagnostic evidence and retains its worker and checkout. No automatic Git integration, pushes or deployment. The source snapshot and branch remain reviewable.

## Verification

Build and 102 core tests passed. Tests cover correction to Done, bounded repeated failure, legacy verification-question recovery with agent attribution, and existing mandatory-human and question behavior. The installed service actually resumed Sol on #17 as attempt 2 without human impersonation. The main checkout and index remain preserved.

before.body:
## Intended outcome

Let a designated reviewer/orchestrator agent coordinate workers through Control Room, independently review their submissions, accept satisfactory work into Done, and escalate work that needs human judgment or feedback. The human sees a clear account of who is doing what and why work was accepted or escalated.

## Requested workflow

1. Orchestrator decomposes permitted work into tickets, adds acceptance criteria/dependencies/context and assigns a named worker.
2. Worker acknowledges/claims the assignment, works in its checkout, reports progress or blockers, and submits a handoff plus verification evidence to Review.
3. Orchestrator inspects the implementation against the acceptance criteria, applicable decisions and UI rules. It checks the submitted code state and performs independent verification where appropriate.
4. Orchestrator records one of three outcomes: Accept into Done; Request changes with actionable feedback; Needs human with a specific question or review request.
5. Human responses return the ticket to the appropriate worker/reviewer queue without losing the prior review history. Humans can override/reopen outcomes.

## Proposed product rules

- Keep worker, orchestrator and human roles distinct. Agents remain attributed as agents and never impersonate a human to accept work. Human explicitly designates an orchestrator and can revoke its authority. The existing human-review workflow remains the default unless orchestration is enabled.
- Worker submissions do not self-approve. Record assignment, worker identity, reviewer identity, outcome, rationale, acceptance criteria checked, evidence and reviewed code state separately. Flag cases where the reviewer also performed implementation for independent/human review.
- Delegation uses durable assignments separate from expiring execution claims. Assigned does not mean acknowledged, claimed does not prove running, and expired claims do not silently free an active worker's checkout. Reassignment preserves history and handles late submissions explicitly.
- Review decisions take the ticket revision and the submitted code/evidence identity. Changed submissions require fresh review. A green test alone is not proof of the intended outcome. Missing or stale evidence must be resolved or escalated.
- Needs human is explicit routing of a question/review, not an ambiguous blocker string. Explain what the human must decide, show the relevant diff/screenshot/evidence, and preserve any unsent feedback. Human-required tickets cannot be quietly auto-accepted.
- Acceptance is separate from Git operations. Do not implicitly merge, push or deploy when accepting a ticket. Where the project defines integration as part of Done, verify the integrated result before acceptance.
- Parent completion remains a deliberate outcome review, not automatic completion when children close.
- Show the agent roster, assigned/claimed work, review queue, Needs human queue, review outcome badges and acceptance history in the UI. Keep authoritative records readable in Markdown.
- Expose matching CLI/MCP operations and role-specific context/protocols so different models and coding tools can participate.
- Identity labels are workflow attribution for agents sharing the local account; they are not a strong isolation/security boundary.

## Confirmed interview choices

- Control Room should launch and supervise coding agents itself. This is in scope for the first version, not merely assigning tickets to manually running agents.
- The orchestrator may start/decompose/reprioritize work only within human-approved goals or tickets. It cannot approve new scope for itself.

## Pending interview choices

- First supported coding tools: Codex CLI and Claude Code, or one initially.
- Integration: orchestrator merges into a configured development branch after verification, or leaves accepted work for a human to merge.
- Mandatory human-review policy: design/product/architecture decisions; explicit ticket requirements plus orchestrator uncertainty; or every parent goal.

These questions are open in the Codex question interface. Do not treat proposed defaults as answers.

## Managed agent lifecycle requirements

Use an adapter per coding tool with structured run events/results where available. Record requested, launching, running, waiting for input, completed, failed, interrupted and unknown/recovery states separately from ticket status. Track run ID, assigned ticket, role/model, checkout/branch, process identity, last event and final result. A process exit does not complete a ticket; a review receipt does.

Allocate isolated worker worktrees, limit concurrent runs, honor ticket dependencies and surface overlapping work before integration. Persist recoverable run metadata locally; keep credentials out of board records and exports. After service restart, reconcile existing runs instead of blindly launching duplicates. Cancellation must stop the relevant run and leave its worktree/diff and handoff recoverable. Approval prompts, authentication failures, unavailable tools, usage limits and ambiguous exits should become explicit agent/Needs-human states. Add configurable retry/resource limits so blocked work does not spin indefinitely.

The orchestrator should run through the same adapter boundary, consume board events and resume with durable context. No API-provider credential or embedded model subscription is assumed; supported harness setup must be explicit. Worker results are claims to review, not trusted acceptance instructions.

## Implementation outline (proposal)

A. Role/policy configuration, review routing and durable review receipts; preserve existing human behavior and Markdown compatibility.
B. Assignment/acknowledgment/reassignment, worker queues, dependencies and worktree conflict visibility, CLI/MCP protocol.
C. Orchestrator review context and accept/changes/escalate operations, evidence/code identity checks, human-response continuation and parent review.
D. Human dashboard and history, plus a documented end-to-end trial with at least two workers.
E. Launch/supervision adapters and recovery are required in the first version, using the coding tools selected in the interview.

## Acceptance checks

- Two named workers can receive distinct assignments and cannot silently overwrite claims or review decisions.
- A worker cannot accept its own work or grant itself reviewer/scope authority through ordinary workflow operations.
- A designated orchestrator can accept a permitted current submission with an attributed review receipt, request changes, or escalate it with a specific question.
- Human-required work, changed evidence/code, revoked reviewer authority, stale revisions, expired claims, late submissions and retry exhaustion have explicit outcomes.
- Questions do not expire. Human answers, review history, assignments and acceptance receipts survive service restart and Markdown reload.
- The board distinguishes orchestrator-accepted from human-accepted work and exposes any unverified integration state.
- Existing projects retain their current human-only acceptance behavior until orchestration is explicitly enabled.

## Related work and implementation starting points

Related: #58 (human review queue), #28 (reported progress), #31 (decision protocol), #26 (agent playbook). Reuse these rather than creating competing queues/protocols.

Current enforcement lives in src/store.ts assertAgent/reviewOutcome; Actor only distinguishes human/agent in src/types.ts. CLI/MCP and generated context currently promise human-only Done. Update these together when the interview choices are settled. This ticket records the product proposal and confirmed interview choices. Implementation has not started; pending choices are not approved defaults.

On completion, current independent verification plus orchestrator acceptance should move #17 to Done; genuine questions and mandatory human flags should still request your input. This #65 implementation is my own work, so I have not self-accepted it.

meta.title: Bulk edit feature for tickets

before.body:
## Backlog refinement

Prepared by Codex backlog refinement. This describes planned work; implementation has not started.

### Intended outcome

Select multiple tickets and change shared fields in one operation, with predictable selection and a clear result for every ticket.

### Scope and approach

Extend the existing table checkbox/bulk-status UI to status, priority, owner, labels, and parent; expose selection on the board as well. Labels need separate add/remove actions so existing labels are not accidentally replaced. Approval actions are specified in #16; deletion is outside this ticket.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Board and table support explicit multi-selection, select visible items, clear selection, and a persistent count while the action is being prepared.
- [ ] Only selected visible tickets are affected; filtering or changing view reconciles selection and never silently includes hidden items.
- [ ] Mixed values display as Mixed. Fields left unchanged retain their original values; label addition/removal preserves all other labels.
- [ ] Each change uses the ticket’s revision and normal validation, including parent cycles, scope, and review evidence requirements.
- [ ] The result identifies succeeded, failed, and unchanged tickets; failed items remain available for correction/retry without reapplying successful writes.
- [ ] Selection and operations are keyboard accessible and survive ordinary live refresh without jumping to different tickets.

### Implementation notes and related work

web/TableView.tsx currently loops onMove for bulk status changes. Start there and in web/ProjectPage.tsx; coordinate shared selection/results rather than creating a second independent bulk model. Related: #16 and #23.

### Human review / verification

Bulk-edit a mixed selection, add/remove labels, and simulate a stale revision plus a validation failure. Verify exact affected IDs, preservation of untouched fields, and per-item feedback.

meta.title: Bulk edit feature for tickets
meta.handoff: Implemented ticket #17 only. Added shared ID-based selection across board/table, select-visible and clear controls, mixed-value bulk editing for status/priority/owner/parent, additive/removal label operations, per-ticket revision writes, succeeded/failed/unchanged results, and failed-only retry. Fixed parent summaries to show ticket number/title and isolated managed identity variables in tests without changing production enforcement. No decisions recorded; no commit created.
meta.evidence:
`npm run build` passed, including TypeScript, Vite, and CLI bundling.
Managed identity regression passed 1/1 with CONTROLROOM_MANAGED/ACTOR variables present.
Bulk helper regressions passed 3/3.
Prettier check and `git diff --check` passed.
Playwright enumerated all 3 targeted bulk-edit regressions successfully. Runtime browser execution was attempted but this worker sandbox rejects binding 127.0.0.1:4178 with EPERM. The same restriction stops the CLI suite when it reaches service startup; importantly, it advanced beyond both previously failing identity assertions. Controller verification should run the prescribed command and targeted browser tests in its listen-capable environment.

## Backlog refinement

Prepared by Codex backlog refinement. This describes planned work; implementation has not started.

### Intended outcome

Select multiple tickets and change shared fields in one operation, with predictable selection and a clear result for every ticket.

### Scope and approach

Extend the existing table checkbox/bulk-status UI to status, priority, owner, labels, and parent; expose selection on the board as well. Labels need separate add/remove actions so existing labels are not accidentally replaced. Approval actions are specified in #16; deletion is outside this ticket.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Board and table support explicit multi-selection, select visible items, clear selection, and a persistent count while the action is being prepared.
- [ ] Only selected visible tickets are affected; filtering or changing view reconciles selection and never silently includes hidden items.
- [ ] Mixed values display as Mixed. Fields left unchanged retain their original values; label addition/removal preserves all other labels.
- [ ] Each change uses the ticket’s revision and normal validation, including parent cycles, scope, and review evidence requirements.
- [ ] The result identifies succeeded, failed, and unchanged tickets; failed items remain available for correction/retry without reapplying successful writes.
- [ ] Selection and operations are keyboard accessible and survive ordinary live refresh without jumping to different tickets.

### Implementation notes and related work

web/TableView.tsx currently loops onMove for bulk status changes. Start there and in web/ProjectPage.tsx; coordinate shared selection/results rather than creating a second independent bulk model. Related: #16 and #23.

### Human review / verification

Bulk-edit a mixed selection, add/remove labels, and simulate a stale revision plus a validation failure. Verify exact affected IDs, preservation of untouched fields, and per-item feedback.

If the LLM has questions about a ticket, they can add a questionaire with multiple choice questions or text questions to a ticket and mark it as needing human feedback. 

## Backlog refinement

Prepared by Codex backlog refinement. This describes planned work; implementation has not started.

### Intended outcome

Let an agent attach a structured questionnaire to a ticket and request human input, keeping questions and answers in the ticket’s conversation.

### Scope and approach

Support one or more multiple-choice or free-text questions, an explicit needs-feedback state, and answering at the human’s pace. Store structured data durably in Markdown records/metadata and expose it through CLI/MCP context. Keep this distinct from mandatory ticket creation forms.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An agent can submit a questionnaire with stable question IDs, clear prompts, answer types, and optional recommended choices; users can provide custom text where choices are offered.
- [ ] The ticket appears in Needs you with a direct route to its unanswered questionnaire; a separate flag does not silently change its workflow stage.
- [ ] Questions never time out or disappear because the user pauses. Draft answers persist across closing/reopening and refresh, and can be submitted explicitly.
- [ ] No recommended/preselected option counts as an answer until the human submits; required unanswered questions remain visible.
- [ ] Submitted answers retain human attribution, question wording, and timestamps in the conversation, and are readable by agent context and wait-for-update workflows.
- [ ] Question edits/replacements and amended answers retain history; stale submissions do not overwrite a newer questionnaire, and resolving one request does not clear unrelated open questions.

### Implementation notes and related work

Extend src/types.ts, src/store.ts comments/context, src/server.ts, src/cli.ts/src/mcp.ts, web/RecordDetail.tsx and web/model.ts attention handling. Reuse the existing question/resolve flow where possible. Related: #26.

### Human review / verification

Submit a mixed questionnaire, leave it unanswered beyond ordinary UI timers, save a partial draft, reload, and finish later. Confirm that an agent receives the explicit answers and that a concurrent question edit triggers reconciliation.

before.body:
## Backlog refinement

Prepared by Codex backlog refinement. This describes planned work; implementation has not started.

### Intended outcome

Provide a dedicated vertical planning view where dragging tickets changes the order in which work should be considered.

### Scope and approach

Build on the saved table view and existing manual/priority sorting. Offer an obvious Priority planning preset, rank tickets within priority groups, and allow explicit movement into another priority group. Ordering must not silently change workflow status or parent. Explain that priority is the urgency bucket and rank is the order within it.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The planning view shows a vertical list with priority groups and visible drag handles, including the start/end of each group.
- [ ] Dragging within a group changes persistent relative rank; dragging to another priority group updates priority and rank visibly.
- [ ] Reordering across tickets with different statuses does not move either ticket to the other status or change its parent.
- [ ] Move up/down and move-to-priority controls provide keyboard alternatives, including first/last positions.
- [ ] Reloading or returning to the saved view retains the order; concurrent reorder failures reconcile without losing tickets.
- [ ] Filtered reordering uses defined visible anchors and preserves the relative order of hidden tickets; saved sort modes clearly indicate whether manual reordering is active.

### Implementation notes and related work

Start with web/ProjectPage.tsx place/peersOf, web/TableView.tsx and web/model.ts sortTickets. Current place also copies the target status, so reuse needs care. Coordinate drag preview with #22; prefer existing order metadata over a second competing ranking field.

### Human review / verification

Rank tickets across several stages and priorities, move to first/last, refresh, and repeat with a filter and keyboard controls. Confirm that status/parent stay unchanged and priority changes only when crossing an explicit priority group.

before.body:
## Backlog refinement

Prepared by Codex backlog refinement. This describes planned work; implementation has not started.

### Intended outcome

Make workflow status customization easy to discover from the board and safe to use as the project evolves.

### Scope and approach

Settings already supports naming, roles, ordering, addition, and removal of columns. Expose a clear Customize statuses entry from the board and improve that existing editor. Retain stable IDs and explain why workflow roles control agent behavior; multiple columns can share a role, as Concept and Backlog do here.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A user can find status customization from the board, add a status, rename it, and change its order without editing configuration files.
- [ ] Renaming or reordering retains ticket associations, history, and saved views; refreshing preserves the configuration.
- [ ] The editor distinguishes display name from workflow role and validates required roles and invalid/blank names.
- [ ] Removing a populated status offers an explicit destination/migration flow or a clear route to move its tickets first; no tickets are orphaned.
- [ ] Where a role has multiple columns, default destinations for new tickets and agent role-based moves are visible and deterministic.
- [ ] Concurrent configuration changes cause reconciliation feedback rather than silent overwrites.

### Implementation notes and related work

Start with web/Settings.tsx, web/ProjectPage.tsx, src/store.ts updateConfig and role-to-column lookups in src/cli.ts/src/mcp.ts. Extend existing configuration rather than introducing competing status data.

### Human review / verification

Add and rename a status, reorder it, reload, and remove an empty status. Exercise removal with tickets and ambiguous role destinations using Concept/Backlog and In Progress/Failed Review.

## Backlog refinement

Prepared by Codex backlog refinement. This describes planned work; implementation has not started.

### Intended outcome

Show the prospective ticket order while dragging so the user knows where the ticket will land before releasing it.

### Scope and approach

Add a stable insertion preview or displaced-row/card preview to existing board and table reordering. Keep the preview local until drop and share the behavior with the planning view in #21.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] While dragging over reorderable tickets, a clear insertion position updates before mouse release, including above the first and below the last item.
- [ ] Moving between valid positions updates the preview without flicker or repeatedly writing record order.
- [ ] Escape, dropping outside a valid target, and canceled drags restore the original visual order without persisted changes.
- [ ] A successful drop persists the displayed placement; failed/stale saves restore or reconcile the list and show an error.
- [ ] Scrolling during a drag keeps the preview aligned; invalid cross-parent/status operations follow existing explicit rules.
- [ ] Keyboard reorder controls remain available, and reduced-motion settings avoid unnecessary movement.

### Implementation notes and related work

Start with web/BoardView.tsx, web/TableView.tsx, web/TicketCard.tsx and web/ProjectPage.tsx drag/drop handlers; style in web/project.css. Related: #21, but this fixes the existing reorder interaction independently.

### Human review / verification

Observe a drag before release, cancel it, reorder at both ends, and repeat in a long scrollable list. Confirm canceled previews produce no record writes and the saved order matches the preview.

These are just small tasks that are tracked inside the ticket and don't show up as separate full tickets. Sort of like a checklist of things that need to be done for that ticket. 

## Backlog refinement

Prepared by Codex backlog refinement. This describes planned work; implementation has not started.

### Intended outcome

Track small steps inside a ticket with a checklist, without creating separate numbered tickets or cluttering the board.

### Scope and approach

Provide an editable Microtasks section with add, rename, reorder, complete, and remove actions. Keep it readable/editable in Markdown and include it in agent context. Reuse Markdown task-list syntax in a clearly owned section where practical; preserve other prose and existing acceptance criteria.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Enter adds a nonblank checklist item and keeps focus ready for the next; items can be checked, edited, reordered, and removed with keyboard alternatives.
- [ ] Items persist across save/reopen and direct Markdown edits; concurrent changes use revision protection.
- [ ] Agents can read and update checklist state through the supported record interfaces without creating ticket IDs for checklist items.
- [ ] The ticket displays completed/total counts, including the all-complete state; cards may show a compact count without listing every item.
- [ ] Completing the checklist does not automatically move the ticket to Done or claim its acceptance criteria are satisfied.
- [ ] Unrelated Markdown, attachments, and comments survive checklist edits.

### Implementation notes and related work

Start with web/RecordDetail.tsx, web/RecordMarkdown.tsx (GFM rendering already exists), src/files.ts Markdown preservation and src/store.ts context. Related: #14 for work large enough to need child tickets; #23 for reducing board clutter.

### Human review / verification

Create/reorder/toggle items, reopen, edit a task in Markdown, and retrieve agent context. Verify a stale toggle cannot overwrite a newer edit and all-complete leaves ticket status unchanged.

before.body:
I would like a way to click a swimlane and turn on/off the tickets in that swimline from being visible. For example backlog can be large and I want to turn off backlog and just view the other swimlanes. Maybe a little human eye icon that is in the swimlane header you can click and quickly turn on/off visibility.

## Backlog refinement

Prepared by Codex backlog refinement. This describes planned work; implementation has not started. Proposed behavior below remains subject to human scope review.

### Intended outcome

Temporarily hide tickets in a busy status column such as Backlog with one click, then restore them just as easily.

### Scope and approach

The Backlog example refers to workflow/status columns (called swimlanes in the request). Add an eye-style visibility toggle to each column header. Hide that column's ticket content across all parent/label groups, retaining a compact labeled header or equivalent visible restore control. This is a visibility preference, not an archive or ticket-status change.

Proposed default: remember hidden column IDs per project and saved view in personal UI preferences, without rewriting the shared view's search query. Keep visibility independent of existing horizontal group collapse. Provide Show all columns and a clear indication of hidden columns.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] One click hides Backlog's cards across all groups and leaves other columns usable. A visible control restores Backlog with one click.
- [ ] Header controls expose an accessible name and pressed/expanded state, work by keyboard, and clearly distinguish hidden from empty columns.
- [ ] No ticket, claim, stage, archive flag or parent relationship changes when toggling visibility.
- [ ] Search/filter changes compose with visibility without losing the user's query. Hidden columns remain identifiable, and Show all recovers from every column being hidden.
- [ ] Visibility is remembered for that project/view after refresh without leaking to another project/view; custom column rename/reorder preserves it by stable ID, and deleted IDs are safely ignored.
- [ ] Board keyboard navigation skips hidden cards, focus stays recoverable after hiding a focused column, and hidden content cannot receive invisible drag/drop or quick-create interactions.
- [ ] Counts and any bulk-action preview make their scope clear; hidden tickets are not silently selected for operations on visible tickets.
- [ ] Table/list views retain their existing behavior; switching back to the board restores its column visibility preferences.

### Implementation notes and related work

Inspect web/BoardView.tsx column rendering and keyboard navigation, web/ProjectPage.tsx view preferences and web/model.ts filters. Related: #44 quick archive, #23 ticket clutter, #18 status customization. Do not conflate this with existing parent-group collapse or automatically create a new shared saved view.

### Human review / verification

Hide Backlog on a populated parent-grouped board, filter the remaining tickets, restore Backlog and refresh. Switch views/projects and rename a custom column. Check keyboard recovery and the all-hidden state.

This should sort oldest comments first with an icon you can click to change sort order. 

## Backlog refinement

Prepared by Codex backlog refinement. This describes planned work; implementation has not started.

### Intended outcome

Read a ticket’s conversation in chronological order by default, with a simple icon control to switch to newest-first when desired.

### Scope and approach

Default ticket conversations to oldest-first. Add a visible sort-direction icon next to Conversation with a tooltip, accessible name, and current order. Remember the selected preference per project. This controls comments inside a ticket, independently of the newest-first project activity feed in #25.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Opening a conversation without an existing preference shows comments from oldest to newest, ordered by their recorded timestamps rather than filenames or record enumeration order.
- [ ] Clicking the sort control switches between Oldest first and Newest first; all comment types participate in the same consistent order.
- [ ] Equal timestamps use a deterministic secondary key, and changing order neither duplicates nor loses entries.
- [ ] The chosen order persists across closing/reopening and refresh through the project preference model.
- [ ] New comments appear in the correct position without forcing a reader away from older content; after posting, the author can readily find their own new comment.
- [ ] Keyboard users can toggle the icon, and its label/tooltip communicates the current order and available action. Existing comment resolution and review summaries continue to work.

### Implementation notes and related work

Inspect src/store.ts comments enumeration and web/RecordDetail.tsx conversation mapping, plus the existing preference plumbing in web/App.tsx and src/server.ts. Apply presentation sorting without changing stored timestamps or the chronological history available to agents.

### Human review / verification

Use a conversation with mixed comment types, deliberately nonchronological record filenames, and equal timestamps. Check the default, toggle both directions, post a comment, reload, and confirm no entry disappears or changes content.

## Backlog refinement

Prepared by Codex backlog refinement. This describes planned work; implementation has not started. Proposed behavior below remains subject to human scope review.

### Intended outcome

Opening a ticket from Needs you immediately shows the question to answer or the review action to take, without searching a long conversation. Put manual test/feedback instructions beside Accept/Reject.

### Scope and approach

Add a prominent action area near the top of ticket details and conversation views, aligned with the existing review controls. Surface all unresolved questions with their author and original context, with an answer action and a link to the original thread entry. Render this from the existing question records rather than creating duplicate comments. Show the same action area when opening the ticket directly so the need for attention does not depend on the entry route.

For Review tickets, display the current submission's human review instructions, relevant handoff and verification summary beside Accept/Reject. If the submission explicitly requires no manual checks and recorded verification supports it, say the test suite passed and offer the evidence. Never infer a pass or invent manual checks from missing instructions; missing/failed/unrun verification must be clearly labeled.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Opening a question-bearing ticket from Needs you shows the unresolved question text near the top, regardless of conversation sort order or length.
- [ ] Multiple unresolved questions remain individually identifiable with attribution, links to their original entries and a straightforward answer path. Long content can expand without concealing the existence of other questions.
- [ ] Posting an answer uses the existing durable conversation and retains the draft on failure; resolving a question is explicit and affects only that question. Merely opening a ticket never resolves it.
- [ ] Resolving/reopening a question updates the top area and Needs you after refresh; review instructions remain visible if the ticket also awaits review.
- [ ] Review instructions and requested feedback appear beside the existing Accept/Reject controls, with accessible Markdown and useful links. Acceptance feedback continues to work as implemented in #30.
- [ ] The summary reflects the latest review submission and distinguishes manual checks, successful automated verification, failures, exceptions and missing evidence. An old passing result is not presented as proof of a newer unverified submission.
- [ ] When no manual checks are explicitly required and the current submission has passing verification, concise text says the test suite passed, with access to its recorded command/result. Otherwise the UI states what is requested or unknown truthfully.
- [ ] Needs you remains actionable until all applicable attention reasons are addressed; resolving one question does not hide another question or a pending review.
- [ ] Keyboard and compact-screen users can reach the question/answer and review controls without losing unsaved ticket or reply drafts.

### Implementation notes and related work

Inspect web/Pages.tsx AttentionPage, web/model.ts attention reasons, web/RecordDetail.tsx question comments and review data, and web/ReviewActions.tsx. Test a Review ticket with manual steps, one explicitly requiring only recorded automated checks, and one with missing/failed verification. Check that a fresh review submission cannot inherit a misleading old pass summary.

before.body:
## Backlog refinement

Prepared by Codex backlog refinement. This describes planned work; implementation has not started. Proposed behavior below remains subject to human scope review.

### Intended outcome

Navigate directly from a child ticket to its parent without searching the board or using the parent-selection editor.

### Scope and approach

Show a clearly labeled parent link with the parent's ticket number and short title near the top of ticket details. Keep this navigation separate from changing the parent relationship. Follow existing ticket-link behavior, including middle-click and modifier-click opening a separate tab.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A child ticket shows a keyboard-accessible Parent: #number title link; clicking it opens the correct parent's detail dialog.
- [ ] Same-tab navigation saves pending edits first using the existing autosave/conflict behavior. A failed save keeps the child draft open and explains the failure.
- [ ] Middle-click/modifier-click opens the parent in a separate tab while leaving the current ticket and its draft intact; the resulting URL survives refresh.
- [ ] An archived parent remains navigable and is clearly marked Archived; navigation does not unarchive or reparent anything.
- [ ] A ticket without a parent has no misleading navigation target. A missing parent shows an unavailable state without crashing or silently discarding the stored relationship.
- [ ] Changing the parent updates the navigation target consistently after saving. The parent picker continues to edit the relationship independently.
- [ ] Long titles remain usable at compact/mobile widths, with accessible link names that include the ticket number and title.

### Implementation notes and related work

Reuse web/ticketNavigation.ts from #42 and RecordDetail's save-before-child-navigation pattern. Inspect web/RecordDetail.tsx and web/ParentInput.tsx. Related: #14 child management, #15 parent selection, #42 new-tab navigation. Breadcrumb navigation across the full ancestry and a new navigation-history system are outside this scope.

### Human review / verification

Open a child, edit its description and navigate to its parent, then reopen the child to verify persistence. Try keyboard, middle-click, an archived parent, a long title and a failed/conflicting save.

before.body:
## Backlog refinement

Prepared by Codex backlog refinement. This describes planned work; implementation has not started.

### Intended outcome

Select multiple tickets and change shared fields in one operation, with predictable selection and a clear result for every ticket.

### Scope and approach

Extend the existing table checkbox/bulk-status UI to status, priority, owner, labels, and parent; expose selection on the board as well. Labels need separate add/remove actions so existing labels are not accidentally replaced. Approval actions are specified in #16; deletion is outside this ticket.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Board and table support explicit multi-selection, select visible items, clear selection, and a persistent count while the action is being prepared.
- [ ] Only selected visible tickets are affected; filtering or changing view reconciles selection and never silently includes hidden items.
- [ ] Mixed values display as Mixed. Fields left unchanged retain their original values; label addition/removal preserves all other labels.
- [ ] Each change uses the ticket’s revision and normal validation, including parent cycles, scope, and review evidence requirements.
- [ ] The result identifies succeeded, failed, and unchanged tickets; failed items remain available for correction/retry without reapplying successful writes.
- [ ] Selection and operations are keyboard accessible and survive ordinary live refresh without jumping to different tickets.

### Implementation notes and related work

web/TableView.tsx currently loops onMove for bulk status changes. Start there and in web/ProjectPage.tsx; coordinate shared selection/results rather than creating a second independent bulk model. Related: #16 and #23.

### Human review / verification

Bulk-edit a mixed selection, add/remove labels, and simulate a stale revision plus a validation failure. Verify exact affected IDs, preservation of untouched fields, and per-item feedback.

meta.title: Bulk edit feature for tickets
meta.handoff: Implemented ticket #17 only. Added shared ID-based selection across board/table, select-visible and clear controls, mixed-value bulk editing for status/priority/owner/parent, additive/removal label operations, per-ticket revision writes, succeeded/failed/unchanged results, and failed-only retry. Fixed parent summaries to show ticket number/title and isolated managed identity variables in tests without changing production enforcement. No decisions recorded; no commit created.

The same restriction stops the CLI suite when it reaches service startup; importantly, it advanced beyond both previously failing identity assertions. Controller verification should run the prescribed command and targeted browser tests in its listen-capable environment.

## Backlog refinement

Prepared by Codex backlog refinement. This describes planned work; implementation has not started.

### Intended outcome

Select multiple tickets and change shared fields in one operation, with predictable selection and a clear result for every ticket.

### Scope and approach

Extend the existing table checkbox/bulk-status UI to status, priority, owner, labels, and parent; expose selection on the board as well. Labels need separate add/remove actions so existing labels are not accidentally replaced. Approval actions are specified in #16; deletion is outside this ticket.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Board and table support explicit multi-selection, select visible items, clear selection, and a persistent count while the action is being prepared.
- [ ] Only selected visible tickets are affected; filtering or changing view reconciles selection and never silently includes hidden items.
- [ ] Mixed values display as Mixed. Fields left unchanged retain their original values; label addition/removal preserves all other labels.
- [ ] Each change uses the ticket’s revision and normal validation, including parent cycles, scope, and review evidence requirements.
- [ ] The result identifies succeeded, failed, and unchanged tickets; failed items remain available for correction/retry without reapplying successful writes.
- [ ] Selection and operations are keyboard accessible and survive ordinary live refresh without jumping to different tickets.

### Implementation notes and related work

web/TableView.tsx currently loops onMove for bulk status changes. Start there and in web/ProjectPage.tsx; coordinate shared selection/results rather than creating a second independent bulk model. Related: #16 and #23.

Bulk-edit a mixed selection, add/remove labels, and simulate a stale revision plus a validation failure. Verify exact affected IDs, preservation of untouched fields, and per-item feedback.

before.body:
## Backlog refinement

Prepared by Codex backlog refinement. This describes planned work; implementation has not started.

### Intended outcome

Make decision documentation a routine part of the agent protocol so consequential project choices and their reasoning are retained beyond the originating ticket.

### Scope and approach

Update tool-neutral agent guidance, generated context, and MCP onboarding to instruct agents to look up existing decisions and create/update decision records when choosing a meaningful architecture, product behavior, UI convention, dependency strategy, or workflow policy. Keep routine implementation trivia out of the decision log.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Instructions state when to record a decision, with examples of consequential choices versus minor implementation details.
- [ ] A decision records the choice, context, rationale, alternatives considered, tradeoffs, scope, attribution, and links to relevant tickets/references.
- [ ] Agents search existing decisions before creating another, link tickets to the applicable decision, and supersede earlier decisions explicitly rather than rewriting away the old rationale.
- [ ] Unresolved proposals and assumptions are labeled as such; an agent does not invent human agreement or treat an unresolved question as an accepted choice.
- [ ] Agents may record decisions within approved work, but decision records do not grant implementation scope approval or bypass human acceptance of tickets.
- [ ] Review handoffs identify decisions made or changed, and agents can retrieve those records after the originating ticket is archived.
- [ ] The instructions ship consistently in AGENT_GUIDE.md, generated context, and MCP guidance; users can see the rule in the playbook from #26.

### Implementation notes and related work

Start with AGENT_GUIDE.md, src/store.ts contextMarkdown and decision validation, src/mcp.ts onboarding/list_knowledge, and existing record create/update APIs. Reuse durable decision records and predecessor links. This is protocol-driven behavior, not automatic inference from arbitrary file changes.

### Human review / verification

Run a disposable agent workflow that makes a meaningful design choice, records its alternatives/rationale, links it to the ticket, and later supersedes it. Confirm the guidance is available through CLI/MCP context and that archived work does not hide its decisions.

## Finding

runVerification converts a null process status to exit code 0 when result.error is absent. A command killed by a signal can therefore be submitted as successful verification and shown as passing in the ticket.

## Reproduction and evidence

In a disposable test, runVerification("kill -TERM $$", temporaryDirectory) returned exitCode: 0 with empty output. The command terminates only its own spawned shell; no application service was affected.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Only an actual normal zero exit is recorded as a pass.

## Finding

The stdio request loop awaits each tool call before reading the next request. A long wait_for_update blocks unrelated reads, claim renewals, pings, and cancellation notifications on the same connection until it finishes.

## Reproduction and evidence

Against a disposable board, sent wait_for_update followed by get_ticket. The lookup remained unanswered while waiting; both responses arrived only after a comment released the wait.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Dispatch independent MCP requests without blocking the input reader and correlate each response with its request ID.
- [ ] get_ticket and ping respond while a wait_for_update request remains pending.
- [ ] Handle cancellation and connection closure so pending waits clean up their event streams and timers.
- [ ] Keep coordinated mutations serialized by the existing shared service and add concurrent-request regression coverage.
